{{short description|Function on an integer n which is log(p) if n equals p^k and zero otherwise}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''von Mangoldt function''' is an [[arithmetic function]] named after [[Germany|German]] mathematician [[Hans Carl Friedrich von Mangoldt|Hans von Mangoldt]]. It is an example of an important arithmetic function that is neither [[multiplicative function|multiplicative]] nor [[additive function|additive]].

==Definition==
The von Mangoldt function, denoted by <math>\Lambda(n)</math>, is defined as

:<math>\Lambda(n) = \begin{cases} \log p & \text{if }n=p^k \text{ for some prime } p \text{ and integer } k \ge 1, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}</math>

The first few values of <math>\Lambda(n)</math> are

:<math>0 , \log 2 , \log 3 , \log 2 , \log 5 , 0 , \log 7 , \log 2 , \log 3, 0, \log 11, 0,\dots </math>

which is related to {{OEIS|id=A014963}}.

==Properties==
The von Mangoldt function satisfies the identity<ref name=Apo32>Apostol (1976) p.32</ref><ref name=Ten30>Tenenbaum (1995) p.30</ref>

:<math>\log(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} \Lambda(d).</math>

The sum is taken over all [[integer]]s {{mvar|d}} that [[division (mathematics)|divide]] {{mvar|n}}.  This is proved by the [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic]], since the terms that are not powers of primes are equal to {{math|0}}.  For example, consider the case {{math|''n'' {{=}} 12 {{=}} 2<sup>2</sup> × 3}}. Then
:<math>\begin{align}
\sum_{d \mid 12} \Lambda(d) &= \Lambda(1) + \Lambda(2) + \Lambda(3) + \Lambda(4) + \Lambda(6) + \Lambda(12) \\
&= \Lambda(1) + \Lambda(2) + \Lambda(3) + \Lambda \left (2^2 \right ) + \Lambda(2 \times 3) + \Lambda \left (2^2 \times 3 \right) \\
&= 0 + \log(2) + \log(3) + \log(2) + 0 + 0 \\
&=\log (2 \times 3 \times 2) \\
&= \log(12).
\end{align}</math>

By [[Möbius inversion formula|Möbius inversion]], we have
:<math>\Lambda (n) = \sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d) \log\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)</math>
where <math>\mu(d)</math> is the [[Möbius function]]. Then by using the [[product rule]] for the logarithm we get<ref name=Ten30/><ref name=Apo33>Apostol (1976) p.33</ref><ref>{{cite book | last=Schroeder | first=Manfred R. | title=Number theory in science and communication. With applications in cryptography, physics, digital information, computing, and self-similarity | edition=3rd | zbl=0997.11501 | series=Springer Series in Information Sciences | volume=7 | location=Berlin | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | year=1997 | isbn=3-540-62006-0 }}</ref>
:<math>\Lambda (n) = - \sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d) \log(d) \ . </math>

For all <math>x\ge 1</math>, we have<ref name=Apo88>Apostol (1976) p.88</ref>
:<math> \sum_{n\le x}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n}=\log x+O(1).</math>
Also, there exist positive constants {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''c''<sub>2</sub>}} such that
:<math> \psi(x)\le c_1x, </math>
for all <math>x\ge 1</math>, and
:<math> \psi(x)\ge c_2x, </math>
for all sufficiently large {{math|''x''}}.

==Dirichlet series==
The von Mangoldt function plays an important role in the theory of [[Dirichlet series]], and in particular, the [[Riemann zeta function]]. For example, one has

:<math>\log \zeta(s)=\sum_{n=2}^\infty \frac{\Lambda(n)}{\log(n)}\,\frac{1}{n^s}, \qquad \text{Re}(s) > 1.</math>

The [[logarithmic derivative]] is then<ref name=HW>Hardy & Wright (2008) §17.7, Theorem 294</ref>

:<math>\frac {\zeta^\prime(s)}{\zeta(s)} = -\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^s}.</math>

These are special cases of a more general relation on Dirichlet series.  If one has

:<math>F(s) =\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{f(n)}{n^s}</math>

for a [[completely multiplicative function]] {{math|''f''(''n'')}}, and the series converges for {{math|Re(''s'') > σ<sub>0</sub>}}, then

:<math>\frac {F^\prime(s)}{F(s)} = - \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{f(n)\Lambda(n)}{n^s}</math>

converges for {{math|Re(''s'') > σ<sub>0</sub>}}.

==Chebyshev function==
The second [[Chebyshev function]] <math>\psi(x)</math> is the [[summatory function]] of the von Mangoldt function:<ref name=Apo246>Apostol (1976) p.246</ref>

:<math> \psi(x) = \sum_{p^k\le x}\log p=\sum_{n \leq x} \Lambda(n) \ . </math>

It was introduced by [[Pafnuty Chebyshev]] who used it to show that the true order of the prime counting function <math>\pi(x)</math> is <math>x/\log x</math>. Von Mangoldt provided a rigorous proof of an explicit formula for <math>\psi(x)</math> involving a sum over the non-trivial zeros of the [[Riemann zeta function]]. This was an important part of the first proof of the [[prime number theorem]].

The [[Mellin transform]] of the Chebyshev function can be found by applying [[Perron's formula]]:

:<math>\frac{\zeta^\prime(s)}{\zeta(s)} = - s\int_1^\infty \frac{\psi(x)}{x^{s+1}}\,dx</math>

which holds for <math>\operatorname{Re}(s)>1</math>.

==Exponential series==
[[File:Mangoldt-series.svg|thumb|right|400px]]

[[G. H. Hardy|Hardy]] and [[J. E. Littlewood|Littlewood]] examined the series<ref>{{Cite journal |first=G. H. |last=Hardy |name-list-style=amp |first2=J. E. |last2=Littlewood |url=http://www.ift.uni.wroc.pl/%7Emwolf/Hardy_Littlewood%20zeta.pdf |title=Contributions to the Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function and the Theory of the Distribution of Primes |journal=Acta Mathematica |volume=41 |year=1916 |pages=119–196 |doi=10.1007/BF02422942 |access-date=2014-07-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120207110455/http://www.ift.uni.wroc.pl/%7Emwolf/Hardy_Littlewood%20zeta.pdf |archive-date=2012-02-07 |url-status=dead |doi-access=free }}</ref>

:<math>F(y)=\sum_{n=2}^\infty \left(\Lambda(n)-1\right) e^{-ny}</math>

in the limit {{math|''y'' → 0<sup>+</sup>}}. Assuming the [[Riemann hypothesis]], they demonstrate that

:<math>F(y)=O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\right)\quad \text{and}\quad F(y)=\Omega_\pm\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\right)</math>

In particular this function is oscillatory with diverging [[oscillation (mathematics)|oscillations]]: there exists a value {{math|''K'' > 0}} such that both inequalities 

:<math>F(y)< -\frac{K}{\sqrt{y}}, \quad \text{ and } \quad F(z)> \frac{K}{\sqrt{z}}</math>

hold infinitely often in any neighbourhood of 0. The graphic to the right indicates that this behaviour is not at first numerically obvious: the oscillations are not clearly seen until the series is summed in excess of 100 million terms, and are only readily visible when {{math|''y'' < 10<sup>−5</sup>}}.

==Riesz mean==
The [[Riesz mean]] of the von Mangoldt function is given by

:<math>\begin{align}
\sum_{n\le \lambda} \left(1-\frac{n}{\lambda}\right)^\delta \Lambda(n) &= -\frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty} 
\frac{\Gamma(1+\delta)\Gamma(s)}{\Gamma(1+\delta+s)} \frac{\zeta^\prime(s)}{\zeta(s)} \lambda^s ds \\
&= \frac{\lambda}{1+\delta} + \sum_\rho \frac{\Gamma(1+\delta)\Gamma(\rho)}{\Gamma(1+\delta+\rho)} + \sum_n c_n \lambda^{-n}.
\end{align}</math>

Here, {{mvar|λ}} and {{mvar|δ}} are numbers characterizing the Riesz mean. One must take {{math|''c'' > 1}}. The sum over {{mvar|ρ}} is the sum over the zeroes of the Riemann zeta function, and

:<math>\sum_n c_n \lambda^{-n}\,</math>

can be shown to be a convergent series for {{math|''λ'' > 1}}.

==Approximation by Riemann zeta zeros==
[[File:Real part of n raised to first zeta zero.svg|thumb|The first Riemann zeta zero wave in the sum that approximates the von Mangoldt function]]

There is an explicit formula for the summatory Mangoldt function <math>\psi(x)</math> given by<ref>{{cite journal|last=Conrey|first=J. Brian|author-link=Brian Conrey|date=March 2003|title=The Riemann hypothesis|url=http://www.ams.org/notices/200303/fea-conrey-web.pdf|journal=Notices Am. Math. Soc.|volume=50|pages=341–353|zbl=1160.11341|number=3}}  Page 346</ref>
:<math>\psi(x)=x-\sum_{\zeta(\rho)=0}\frac{x^\rho}\rho -\log(2\pi).</math>

If we separate out the trivial zeros of the zeta function, which are the negative even integers, we obtain
:<math>\psi(x)=x-\sum_{\zeta(\rho)=0,\ 0<\Re(\rho)<1}\frac{x^\rho}\rho -\log(2\pi)-\frac12\log(1-x^{-2}).
</math>
(The sum is not absolutely convergent, so we take the zeros in order of the [[absolute value]] of their imaginary part.)

In the opposite direction, in 1911 E. Landau proved that for any fixed t > 1<ref>E. Landau, Über die Nullstellen der Zetafunktion, Math. Annalen 71 (1911 ), 548-564.</ref>
:<math>\sum_{0<\gamma \leq T} t^\rho=\frac{-T}{2 \pi} \Lambda(t)+\mathcal{O}(\log T)</math>
(We use the notation ρ = β + iγ for the non-trivial zeros of the zeta function.)
[[File:Von Mangoldt function Fourier transform zeta zero duality.PNG|(Left) The von Mangoldt function, approximated by zeta zero waves.(Right) The Fourier transform of the von Mangoldt function gives a spectrum with imaginary parts of Riemann zeta zeros as spikes.|thumb]]
Therefore, if we use Riemann notation α = −i(ρ − 1/2) we have that the sum over nontrivial zeta zeros expressed as
:<math>\lim _{T \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{T} \sum_{0<\gamma \leq T} \cos (\alpha \log t)=-\frac{\Lambda(t)}{2 \pi \sqrt{t}}</math>
peaks at primes and powers of primes.

The [[Fourier transform]] of the von Mangoldt function gives a spectrum with spikes at ordinates equal to the imaginary parts of the Riemann zeta function zeros. This is sometimes called a duality.

== Generalized von Mangoldt function ==

The functions
:<math>\Lambda_k(n)=\sum\limits_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\log^k(n/d),</math>
where <math>\mu</math> denotes the [[Möbius function]] and <math>k</math> denotes a positive integer, generalize the von Mangoldt function.<ref>{{citation | last1=Iwaniec | first1=Henryk | author-link1=Henryk Iwaniec | last2=Friedlander |first2= John | author-link2=John Friedlander | title=Opera de cribro | publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] | date=2010 | isbn=978-0-8218-4970-5 | mr=2647984 | location=Providence, RI | series=American Mathematical Society Colloquium Publications | volume=57|page=23}}</ref> The function <math>\Lambda_1</math> is the ordinary von Mangoldt function <math>\Lambda</math>.
